cases.note: Why an install was refused. The set this corpus was added for.
The four states a signature can be in, plus the platform gap.
What a package can be.
Sandboxed, or a driver.
Tokens no grant confers (§49.1).
The domains a canonical capability token belongs to (§85.1), in the order §85 lists them.

Every canonical capability token (§85.1), domain by domain: the Standard Robot Interface the Hub has validated robots against, plus the four this document gates a rule on and the interface has no word for — §84's `control.motion`, §49.1's two `hri` tokens and §49.2's `sensing.audio`.
What a string in a capability list can be (§85.1). Four, because *not canonical* has three causes and each has a different fix.
Ordered worst-last; the plan takes the worst binding in it.
Ordered by how much fidelity each costs.
Everything a plan can report about a fit it accepted.
What one channel of a policy output drives.
How a joint is commanded.
The kinds of joint a descriptor can declare.
What a body stands on.
What a sensor produces.
The role vocabulary's chains (§5.1).
The role vocabulary's axes (§5.1).
The motion vocabulary (§84.1), in the order the section lists it. A vendor motion that is none of these declares no canonical motion rather than the nearest one.
What can be wrong with a body's motion list (§84.1).
Ordered by rank. An edition that sorted these would differ on "next tier".
Ordered by strength.
Every guard the kernel can run.
What a tripped guard does.
Where a conformance test runs.
Ordered as the specification lists them.
The operators a §54.2 precondition is written in. One list, or a skill refuses on one robot and runs on another.
Satisfied, unsatisfied, and the third value §54.2 requires: a precondition nobody could evaluate is not a precondition that passed.
Why a predicate could not be decided. §54.2 requires the refusal to name something, and a free-text reason is the same nothing as a free-text precondition.
What can happen to one precondition or success criterion. The fourth is the one the predicate engine does not have: there was no predicate to ask about.
Publisher or site. §54.2: the operator may add preconditions; the skill may not remove them.
Before the skill starts, and every cycle while it runs.
How a skill invocation ends. The Hub's `EpisodeOutcome` and not a second vocabulary, so an aborted skill becomes a labelled training example rather than a gap.
Why a call graph is refused at install (§54.5).

What can be wrong with a cell descriptor (§55.2). Two of them — an unaddressable fact key and one that shadows a derived fact — could not have been named before §54.2 gave `env.*` a path vocabulary to be wrong in.

How a `time_to_safe_state_s` was arrived at (§87.2). Two, and there is no third: `live` is deliberately absent, because a figure a navigation stack supplies per cycle puts a planner inside §36's reserve arithmetic and makes navigation a safety-relevant component with no tier.

What can be wrong with a safe-state declaration (§87.2). `basis_refused` is separate from `basis_unknown` on purpose: a vendor who writes `live` has proposed the design the section rejected, and a refusal reading *unknown basis* would send them to check their spelling.
How a console session reached the robot (§87.4). A route is not a role: §5.1's four are about authority and this is about latency, so a relayed operator is an operator.

§39.1's table as a vocabulary, ordered least to most, with the unauthenticated caller first because §39.1 puts it there — *"the stop control requires no authentication"* is the one rule in that section with an injury behind it.

What somebody may ask a console to do (§39.1, §87.4), in the order a console draws them. `stop_request` is first and is §39.1's *stop* row renamed: over a relay there is no latency bound to promise, and a control that looks like an estop and is not one is the hazard §87.4 refuses to build.

Three rather than two, and the third is §80's `inert` precedent: a session refused at open needs a deadline written into the profile and one that expired needs a reconnection, so folding them together produces the single unhelpful sentence.
Why a session holds nothing (§87.4). A relay session with no deadline is the one that matters — it is what gives the decision teeth rather than a paragraph.
Why one action is refused to a session that exists (§87.4). The role is read before presence, because being an observer is the fact that would still be true if they walked over to the robot.

Why a motion request was refused (§88.2), in evaluation order. Authority before state, state before content: a request from a holder that does not hold the body is refused without the platform reading what it asked for.

§27's states in which a body will run a program (§88.2). `degraded` is among them and that is not a softening: §27 puts it on a body that is still there and still answering, and §36.3 is an entire ladder about a robot that keeps working while giving things up.
Whether a motion in flight is still inside its deadline (§88.3). Two words, because §7.1's watchdog has nothing to watch on this path and this is what replaces it.
§27's five states plus §48.1's two, ordered least capable first — the order `evaluate` descends through its rules.

Why the machine is where it is. One per rule, in rule order, because two rules produce `hold` and only the reason tells an operator which one — "a guard asked for a hold" and "there is nothing to run" are the same state and different errands.
§27's four causes of a controlled stop, and no fifth. Closed on purpose: a fifth cause is a fifth thing that stops a robot.
§48.2's report rolled up to the one input §27's machine takes from it. Three rather than §48.4's four outcomes, because the four are per check.
Whether a body knows where its joints are (§48.3).
Present, degraded, lost. The last is separate from the middle because the difference between them is the whole of SAFE.
Nothing to run, something that is not ready, and a lease granted with a plan resolved.
Live or down. §27: "a robot with a policy and no kernel must not exist".
§54.4's stages. `terminal` is one phase rather than three, because the outcome that distinguishes the diagram's three arrows is `skill_outcomes` — the Hub's `EpisodeOutcome`, not a second vocabulary.

Why an invocation is where it is. Four of these end in `terminal` with `aborted`, and only the reason tells an operator whether to call the publisher, look at the cell, find the package holding the arm, or read the black box.

§25.2's arbitration, as the one fact the lifecycle needs from it — deliberately not a copy of the supervisor's richer outcome, because two definitions of a lease result is §31.2's failure in miniature.

What an OS bundle may declare that it changes — the stack §3 draws, and nothing invented beyond it. Two entries carry a rule; the rest are here so that an unrecognised name is recognisable as unrecognised.
§12’s two names. Not the whole rule — an unrecognised component is gated too — which is why this set is frozen beside `os_components` rather than instead of it.
Everything §12 can find wrong with an image, in the order the checks run.
What a supervisor may tell a bootloader, weakest action first. `wait` is the default and the only one of the four that is safe to reach by accident.

Why eight characters are not a pairing code, in the order the checks run. The order is the content: a credential is recognised before a length, which is what keeps `skd_x` from being reported as three missing characters.

§17’s and §57’s device-facing routes, one scope each. This edition’s reading and a default rather than a derived constant — the Hub has declared no vocabulary. The **direction** is not a default: it is an allow-list, and §19’s "assumed lost" is why.
Where a device private key lives (§10).
Everything §10 can find about a robot’s identity, in the order the checks run.
The three states one of §10’s three digests can be in. `nothing` and `unmeasured` are two entries for §37.1’s reason: two facts with two different people at the end of them.
Everything §50 can find about a certificate, in the order of their cost. The first is about the document rather than the machine, which is the order a reader needs.
§50.2’s bindings, in the order that section lists them. Written down once so that a decoder and whatever eventually issues a certificate cannot disagree about which fields are required.
What a birth certificate must never carry. Ownership is established by pairing, by a different party (§50.2).
§56.2’s three classes, strongest to weakest. The order is the ranking, and an edition that sorted these alphabetically would put `field` after `unattested`.
Everything a classification can carry, in the order the checks run.

What a robot may claim about the generation it was given. Four rather than §17’s boolean, because "not applied" covers a robot that is working, one that is waiting for a person, and one whose supervisor disagrees with itself.
§33.4’s six ordered stages, as a check-in names them. Frozen because a fleet console groups by them, and six spellings of one stage is six columns.
§33.6’s four. `stalled` and `unknown` are the pair that carries the section: one is a policy that has stopped producing and the other is one that has not started.

The aggregate health fields, in the order §33.6 lists them. Every one is a key on every check-in whether or not it was measured, so a console iterates the set rather than discovering which of them a robot happened to have.
Everything §11’s pull can find wrong with a desired state it was handed, in the order the checks run. Two refuse and two report, and which is which is the content of the set.
§74’s closed set of counters. Frozen because a fleet console divides by these, and six spellings of one counter is six columns that each look empty.
§36.1's four, plus the fifth §36.1 does not have. Ordered most capable first, which is the order a console renders a fleet in — and `unmetered` is last because it is not a rung of the same ladder.
Why a robot is in the power state it is in, in rule order. The brownout override is first because it is the one rule that ignores a reading it has.

Everything §36 can find wrong with the power subsystem itself, as distinct from a level of charge. Two of the eight raise DEGRADED and five withhold leases, and an edition that agreed about the states could still disagree about which — so the set is frozen alongside them.
§36.3's three levels.
§36.3's ladder, weakest claim first. Order **is** the agreement here: an edition that sorted this alphabetically would give up the black box before the OTA download and the policy loop before either.
The three §36.3 never gives up, at any pressure. Frozen so that "never" is something a test can check rather than a word in a comment.
§36.2's three terms, in that section's order. Two of them have no source anywhere on this platform, which is why they are reported as unaccounted rather than silently omitted.
Everything §74 can find wrong with a window. Three refuse it and one reports — the clock skew is a fact about the robot rather than a reason to discard a measurement.

§79’s eight, in the order the tests run — which is the order of cost, as `planFetch`’s seven are. The two sets are deliberately not the same: `probe` exists because the partial is on the other machine, and `restart` is `discard_and_fetch` for bytes this robot cannot delete.

What the receiver can turn out to hold. The same four names as a bundle’s check and one different remedy — `restart` says what this robot does next, never what the receiver should do with what it has.
§12’s seven, in the order of cost. Frozen alongside §79’s so an edition that agreed about one direction and not the other is a failure rather than a footnote.
What arrived, in the order the checks run. Size before digest, because a short file is a link that dropped and a wrong file is a question about where it came from.

Everything a frame pool can refuse, in the order a reader meets them: the two that say the handle names nothing here, the two that say the loan is not the reader’s to take, and the one that is not a refusal of the reader at all — `pool_exhausted` is capture being told it may not stall.

Where a stream is read (§89): between cycles on the control thread, on a thread of its own because its sensor declares `concurrent_read`, or not at all because its reads kept costing the period — the one of the three that is terminal for the run.
